strengths: The paper studies an important problem—length extrapolation—and the combination of sparse attention, adaptive logit scaling, and hybrid positional encoding is practically interesting.

The synthetic evaluation covers several distinct capabilities, including retrieval, copying, local memory, reversal, and sorting, with extrapolation to substantially longer sequences than used during training.
ASEntmax with NAPE produces striking results on MQMTAR and Reverse, and the tables include useful comparisons against softmax, scalable softmax, fixed entmax, and multiple positional encodings.
The paper is generally well organized and provides extensive appendices, task descriptions, ablations, and attention visualizations.
weaknesses: Several central theoretical claims are not established by the presented arguments. In the over-squashing analysis, the number of paths through L dense attention layers is generally combinatorial/exponential in L rather than O(nL), and the support sets used to trace gradients appear to reverse the query-key dependency. Merely reducing the number of paths also does not imply stronger gradients without controlling path weights, cancellations, and derivatives of attention coefficients.

The positional-encoding theory contains serious gaps. The NoPE analysis assumes a layer-independent geometric decay constant without deriving a uniform bound and reasons about strongly connected components in a causal graph, which is acyclic under the usual orientation. The claim that deleting paths in one layer permanently zeros cumulative influence is not generally valid for products of changing attention matrices.

The RoPE propositions incorrectly reason about individual frequency components as if entmax thresholded each component separately; entmax instead thresholds the summed query-key logit. Consequently, the claimed frequency-specific cutoffs do not follow. The ALiBi proof also mixes the entmax threshold with its rescaled version, including an inconsistent single-support threshold equation.

The representational-preservation result is only an existential counterexample under highly controlled embeddings and simplified attention dynamics. It does not justify the broader language that entmax prevents representational collapse in general transformers, and the extension from the one-layer construction to the stated multilayer architecture is insufficiently supported.

The strongest evidence is confined to small synthetic transformers. The 120M-parameter language-model experiment only fits scaling curves to learned per-position parameters and reports no language-model quality, long-context retrieval, downstream performance, or efficiency measurements. Thus the claimed relevance to practical long-context modeling remains unverified.

Experimental reporting is statistically weak: the paper reports the single best model across three seeds and multiple learning rates, gives no variance, and selects checkpoints using performance at an OOD length that is also part of the reported evaluation regime. This can substantially inflate extrapolation results. The searched learning rates, training duration, validation separation, and per-method tuning budgets are not fully specified.

The empirical gains are not uniformly attributable to ASEntmax: NAPE alone accounts for much of the improvement, fixed entmax is frequently worse than softmax, and ASEntmax degrades performance on several tasks. The paper would need controlled component ablations, matched tuning, aggregate results across seeds, and real-data experiments to support its broad conclusions.
No code or complete reproducibility package is identified, and important implementation details and computational costs are missing despite reliance on specialized sparse-attention kernels.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: length extrapolation in transformer attention, and the intuition that exact zeros can prevent irrelevant tokens from accumulating probability mass is compelling.
ASEntmax is a relatively simple, differentiable modification of entmax, while NAPE provides a practical combination of content-oriented and locality-oriented attention heads.
The experiments span several synthetic tasks, positional encodings, attention transformations, and extrapolation factors. The reported gains on MQMTAR and Reverse are substantial.
The manuscript is generally well organized and includes extensive appendices, task specifications, hyperparameters, and additional results.
weaknesses: Several central theoretical claims are unsupported or incorrect. The representational-preservation argument establishes only a specially constructed one-layer counterexample, yet the paper states a general result after L transformer layers and broadly claims that entmax prevents collapse.

The over-squashing proposition does not prove stronger gradients: reducing the number of nonzero paths alone cannot establish reduced gradient attenuation, and the displayed upper bound provides no lower bound on gradient magnitude. The support/path sets in the proof also appear to reverse the direction of attention dependencies.

The NoPE analysis contains major logical errors. Having a path to the first token in every layer is insufficient for cumulative attention to converge to that token, and deleting a path in one layer does not generally make its cumulative contribution permanently zero. The strongly connected-component discussion is also ill-suited to a causal attention graph.

The ALiBi and RoPE propositions rely on unjustified threshold manipulations. In particular, the ALiBi proof derives a general threshold bound from a hypothetical single-support case, while the RoPE analysis applies the entmax threshold separately to frequency components even though thresholding operates on their summed logit. Dependence of the threshold on alpha is ignored when asserting monotonicity.

The evaluation protocol substantially compromises the evidence: the authors select checkpoints using performance at an out-of-distribution length, report the single best model across three seeds and multiple learning rates, and provide neither means nor variances. This permits test-length leakage and selection bias, especially for unstable extrapolation results.

The empirical scope is almost entirely synthetic. The 120M-parameter FineWeb experiment reports only how well a proposed scaling curve fits learned positional scalars—not language-modeling quality or long-context performance—and even that fit has a weak overall R-squared of 0.17. Consequently, claims about long-context modeling more broadly are not supported.

The source of the gains is insufficiently isolated. NAPE alone makes several tasks essentially trivial for every attention method, fixed entmax often underperforms softmax, and ASEntmax is worse on multiple settings. Although some variants are included, there is no systematic factorial ablation establishing independent contributions from sparsity, adaptive scaling, and positional encoding.

The paper provides no uncertainty estimates, complete search spaces, or code/resource release information despite training on 10–50 million synthetic examples per task. This limits both reproducibility and confidence in the very large headline improvements.

No runtime, memory, realized support-size, or throughput evaluation is provided, so suggestions that sparse attention improves computational efficiency are unsubstantiated. Overall, serious flaws in the theory and evaluation affect the paper's central claims rather than being minor correctable omissions.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem and proposes a simple, practically compatible modification: per-head, content-dependent scaling of α-entmax attention.
The synthetic evaluation is broad, covering retrieval, copying, local memory, reversal, sorting, and flip-flop tasks over unusually large extrapolation factors.
Several empirical gains are striking. In particular, ASEntmax with NAPE substantially outperforms softmax, scalable-softmax, and fixed entmax on MQMTAR and Reverse at extreme lengths.
The paper usefully studies interactions among attention sparsity, temperature scaling, and positional encoding, rather than treating them independently.
The presentation is generally clear, and the appendix supplies extensive task definitions, hyperparameters, additional comparisons, and attention visualizations.
weaknesses: Several central theoretical claims are not established. The over-squashing argument shows fewer nonzero computational paths, but an upper-bound/path-count calculation does not imply stronger gradients or less over-squashing; no gradient lower bound or comparative guarantee is proved.

The non-dispersion result is largely conditional: entropy is small if entmax already has sublinear support, but the paper does not establish that trained entmax attention has such support as length grows. Existence of favorable bounded-logit sequences is much weaker than the broad long-context claim.

The positional-encoding theory contains serious gaps. In the NoPE analysis, connectivity at every layer does not provide the uniform contraction needed for the claimed limit, and deleting paths in one layer does not generally erase earlier token influence from the cumulative attention product. The RoPE component-wise threshold analysis is also not sufficient because attention logits sum contributions from all frequency components.

The representational-preservation claim is only an existential counterexample under highly constructed embeddings and simplified projections, not a general prevention of collapse. The main-text statement using an arbitrary constant c is stronger than what the appendix establishes.

The evaluation protocol risks substantial test-set overfitting: checkpoints are selected using performance at an OOD length, and the paper reports the single best result across three seeds and multiple learning rates rather than means, variances, or a validation-selected model. The searched learning rates and per-seed results are not reported.

Most improvements conflate ASEntmax with the newly introduced NAPE positional scheme. Although component comparisons are provided, a systematic factorial ablation with uncertainty is missing, and NAPE alone explains perfect or near-perfect extrapolation on several tasks.

Evidence is almost entirely from small synthetic models. The 120M-parameter FineWeb experiment only motivates the scaling functional form; it does not evaluate ASEntmax language-model quality, long-context retrieval, downstream accuracy, efficiency, or stability. Thus, the broad implications for practical long-context modeling and LLMs remain unsupported.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or artifact availability is stated, results lack confidence intervals, several tuning ranges are unspecified, and computational or wall-clock comparisons with dense attention are absent.

strengths: The paper studies an important problem and proposes a simple, practically implementable extension of α-entmax with content- and length-dependent, per-head logit scaling.
The empirical scope is substantial: multiple synthetic tasks, positional-encoding variants, a 420M-parameter language model trained on 7B tokens, long-document perplexity, and RULER retrieval.

Several results are genuinely strong, including 95.3% MQMTAR exact match at 65K versus 3.0% for softmax, improved long-context perplexity, and 97.4% S-NIAH-1 accuracy at 16K after 2K-context training.

The paper includes useful comparisons with softmax, scalable softmax, fixed entmax, top-k attention, adaptive-temperature softmax, and stick-breaking attention, and it openly reports tasks where ASEntmax does not dominate.
weaknesses: The central over-squashing result is technically incorrect. With branching factor s over L layers, the number of possible paths is generally exponential in depth, O(s^L), rather than O(sL); the analogous dense count is not O(nL). Moreover, row-wise sparse attention does not bound how many later queries can depend on a given token, and fewer paths alone does not establish stronger gradients. The provided upper bound cannot support the claimed alleviation. Other theoretical claims are also insufficiently justified. The representation-preservation proposition is essentially an existential one-layer construction but is presented as a depth-L transformer result. The NoPE argument assumes that deleting paths in one layer permanently removes cumulative influence, which need not hold through alternative paths. The RoPE analysis applies entmax thresholds to individual frequency components even though thresholding acts on their summed logit, and it drops sine terms without a valid error bound. The ALiBi derivation also uses inconsistent threshold parameterization.

The non-dispersion result is much weaker than the presentation suggests: concentration resilience is existential and the entropy bound H≤log|S| is generic for any sparse distribution. Softmax dispersion additionally assumes logits and temperature remain uniformly bounded with length, excluding precisely the length-dependent scaling baselines under comparison. These results do not establish that learned entmax attention will retain bounded support or generalize.

The synthetic evaluation protocol leaks OOD information: checkpoints are selected using performance at 8× training length, or at 2×/4× when 8× fails. The paper then reports the single best model across three seeds and multiple learning rates rather than means and variability. This can substantially inflate the headline extrapolation results and prevents a statistically fair comparison.

The language-model experiments report no repeated runs, uncertainty, or matched-compute analysis. Since many downstream scores are near random and only two RULER task variants are evaluated, the real-world evidence is narrower than the broad long-context claims suggest.

No support-size trajectories, attention sparsity statistics, throughput, memory use, or end-to-end latency are reported. Exact zeros do not automatically yield computational savings, so the practical cost of replacing optimized softmax attention remains unclear. Reproducibility is also incomplete because the displayed code-availability statement contains no usable link.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem and proposes a simple, implementable combination of sparse entmax attention with learnable, head- and content-dependent length scaling.

The experimental scope is substantial: several synthetic tasks, positional-encoding ablations, 420M-parameter language models trained on 7B tokens, and comparisons with softmax, scalable softmax, fixed entmax, top-k, adaptive-temperature, and stick-breaking baselines.

ASEntmax gives impressive results in selected settings, notably 95.3% exact match at 1024× training length on NAPE-based MQMTAR, near-perfect S-NIAH-1 retrieval at 16K after 2K-context training, and the best reported long-context perplexities.
The paper is generally readable and provides extensive task definitions, hyperparameters, detailed result tables, and some mechanistic diagnostics.
weaknesses: A central theoretical result about over-squashing is incorrect. With branching support s across L layers, the number of possible paths is generally exponential in depth, on the order of s^(L-1), not O(sL); the analogous dense count is not O(nL). The proof also reverses the attention-support relation when describing which later tokens receive influence from an earlier token. Consequently, Proposition 2/4 and the claimed theoretical explanation for stronger gradients do not follow.

The NoPE analysis is not established. The existence of a path in every layer is insufficient to guarantee convergence of products of time-varying stochastic matrices without uniform mixing assumptions. Conversely, deleting paths in one layer does not generally force the cumulative coefficient to remain zero thereafter. The argument involving strongly connected components is also inappropriate for the causal graph as presented.

The RoPE propositions threshold individual frequency components even though entmax thresholds the total query-key score. The small-angle derivation discards sine terms and assumes a positive quadratic decay without sufficient conditions; its denominator can have unsuitable signs. The claimed component-specific cutoffs and monotonic dependence on alpha therefore do not follow.

The representational-preservation result is only an existential counterexample and does not show that bounded-support entmax generally prevents collapse. Its derivation treats essentially a one-layer attention construction while the stated proposition concerns an arbitrary L-layer transformer with residual and feed-forward components. This is much weaker than the paper's broad claims.

The synthetic evaluation has serious test-selection leakage: checkpoints, learning rates, and seeds are selected using performance at out-of-distribution lengths, including 8× test length, and only the single best run is reported. No means, variances, or independently held-out selection lengths are provided. This substantially undermines the headline length-generalization results.

ASEntmax's motivation is weakly validated. The free per-position scaler experiment is only post-hoc fit by the proposed functional form, whose overall R² is reported as merely 0.17. Moreover, softplus cannot attain beta=0 at finite parameters despite the claim that this exactly recovers ordinary entmax, and negative gamma makes the expression problematic at log(n)=0.

The practical evidence is narrower and less consistent than the conclusions imply. ASEntmax is not uniformly best across synthetic tasks or RoPE/ABF settings; S-NIAH-2 accuracy is only 25.4% at 8× context; several short-context benchmarks are near random; and there are no broader long-context language-understanding evaluations, larger-scale models, or statistical uncertainty estimates.

The paper provides no latency, memory, throughput, or realized sparsity measurements. Thus it does not establish practical efficiency benefits despite motivating sparse attention partly as a long-context solution.

Several conclusions conflate conditional or existential facts with guarantees: entropy is bounded only if support is already assumed sublinear, and showing that entmax can ignore appended low-logit tokens does not establish that learned attention will do so under distribution shift.

Given the invalid central theory and compromised model-selection protocol, the main causal and generalization claims are not sufficiently supported for acceptance, despite promising empirical observations.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and offers a coherent central idea: combining the exact sparsity of alpha-entmax with learned, head- and input-dependent length scaling.

The empirical results are broad and often striking. ASEntmax substantially improves extreme-length extrapolation on MQMTAR and Reverse and performs strongly on 420M-parameter language modeling, long-context perplexity, and RULER retrieval.

The comparisons include softmax, fixed entmax, Scalable Softmax, top-k attention, adaptive-temperature softmax, and several positional-encoding configurations. The appendices also provide extensive task definitions, hyperparameters, and additional results.
The paper clearly illustrates that fixed entmax can become excessively sparse and that adaptive scaling can recover performance, providing useful practical insight beyond simply replacing softmax.
weaknesses: The synthetic evaluation has serious selection bias: checkpoints are selected using performance at out-of-distribution test lengths, and the paper reports the single best model across three seeds and multiple learning rates rather than means and uncertainty. This test-set tuning directly affects the headline 1000x-extrapolation claims.

The theoretical claims are substantially stronger than the results. The entropy analysis only establishes that entmax can remain concentrated when its support is already sublinear; it does not show that learned transformer attention will satisfy this condition. Likewise, an existence counterexample does not justify the broad claim that entmax prevents representational collapse.

The over-squashing argument is not convincing. Fewer nonzero paths alone does not imply better sensitivity or stronger useful gradients and can instead remove essential long-range paths. Moreover, the support sets used in the proof appear directionally mis-indexed for causal attention: an input token affects later query j when it belongs to S_j, not when j belongs to the input token's support.

The representational-preservation proof explicitly analyzes essentially a one-layer attention construction but states a result for depth-L transformers with normalization and feed-forward blocks; the extension to the stated architecture is not adequately established.

The language-model evidence is based on one modest scale, apparently single runs without uncertainty, only 7B training tokens, and two RULER subtasks. Broader long-context benchmarks and stronger recent sparse or retrieval-attention baselines are needed to establish generality.

No runtime, memory, or end-to-end throughput measurements are reported. Exact sparsity does not by itself provide computational savings, so the practical efficiency of ASEntmax relative to optimized softmax attention remains unclear.

The contribution is moderately incremental—combining known entmax attention with a generalized learned log-length scaling rule—and the methodological novelty is not strong enough to outweigh the evaluation leakage and unresolved theoretical issues. Overall, the paper is promising but slightly below the acceptance threshold in its current form.
